keyVerseText: And he brought him forth abroad, and said, Look now toward heaven, and tell the stars, if thou be able to number them: and he said unto him, So shall thy seed be.
rootMeaning: The Hebrew word כֹּה (kôh) originates from the prefix k combined with the pronoun הוּא (hûwʼ), which means 'he,' 'it,' or 'that.' This etymology reveals that כֹּה carries a demonstrative force, literally pointing to 'like this' or 'in this manner.' Unlike a simple English adverb, its root connects the manner or place it describes directly to a specific referent, emphasizing immediacy or exactness in the way or position indicated.
usageInScripture: With 573 occurrences, כֹּה is frequently used to express manner, place, or time, often translated as 'thus,' 'here,' or 'so.' Its usage spans indicating how something is done ('thus'), where something is located ('here'), or when something happens ('until now' or 'meanwhile'). The variety of top translations such as 'thus,' 'here,' 'and that way,' and 'on the other side' reflect its flexibility but consistent role as a pointer to a specific manner, place, or time.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding כֹּה enriches our grasp of biblical communication, highlighting God's precision in revelation. When Scripture uses כֹּה, it directs attention to the exact manner or timing of divine action or command, underscoring the faithfulness and intentionality of God's word. This precision invites believers to trust not only the content but the way in which God reveals His promises and instructions, affirming that His dealings are neither vague nor accidental but purposeful and clear. Recognizing this deepens our confidence in Scripture as the authoritative and living word of God.
keyVerseReflection: In Genesis 15:5, God says to Abram, 'So shall thy seed be,' using כֹּה to convey the certainty and manner of the promise. The word emphasizes that the multitude of Abram's descendants will be exactly as God declares—countless and assured. This use of כֹּה assures the believer that God's promises are not abstract but are to be understood as concrete realities spoken with divine authority and certainty.
